chapters.title: Chapter 14 · Good Work
chapters.artPrompt: a young woman in a plain coat and a small girl in a pinafore climbing dark tenement stairs with a basket of bread, a soup pot and a bundle of sewing, a thin seamstress rising from her worktable by a dim window to open the door, gray winter evening light, gentle storybook illustration

blocks.text: Not far from Polly’s lodging lived a seamstress who sewed her eyes sore for other people’s finery. She had little bread for herself. Polly found her out, as she found out everyone poor and shy within reach. First it was a basket of soup. Then it was mending done in return. Then it was an hour of reading aloud. The seamstress said that was better than all the tonics in the city. And the tonics cost more.
The stairs are dark, the basket is heavy, and somebody is glad to see them.

Maud went along on Saturdays, carrying her share of the basket with great solemnity. At first she pitied the seamstress from a kind little height. Then she heard the woman laugh, and saw her mend beautiful things. She came home thoughtful. “She is poor,” Maud reported, “but she is not a beggar. She is a worker, like Tom.” Polly said that was the best lesson Maud had learned all year. And Maud looked as pleased as if it were a prize.
New word: seamstress — a woman who sews for a living, stitch by stitch, often for very little pay.

The strange arithmetic of kindness soon showed itself. When Polly was down with a hard cold one gray spring week, the seamstress climbed her stairs with broth. She mended Maud’s torn coat without one word of thanks wanted. Kindness, Polly said, is like bread: it rises, if you give it time and warmth. The small room had proved it, and so had the small girl. Maud began saving her pocket money that very week, and would not say for what. The seamstress taught her a hemming stitch in return. Maud hemmed everything in the house, and was proud for weeks. The seamstress sewed wedding clothes for the rich, and never once envied them, which Maud noticed before she understood it. It was a kind of riches that could not be stolen.

chapters.title: Chapter 15 · Grandma's Lamp
chapters.artPrompt: a silver-haired grandmother in a lace cap knitting by a small lamp in a cozy corner room, a young woman in a plain dress listening at her feet with sewing in her lap, a sleeping cat, a round table with tea things, deep warm evening light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: The warmest corner of the small Shaw house was Grandma’s room. An old lady sat knitting there by a little lamp, with a cat and a kettle for company. Every evening somebody drifted in. Fanny came with her troubles, Maud with her dolls, Tom with his Sunday papers, Polly with her sewing. Grandma never asked questions. She only made room on the rug, and the questions came of themselves. Nobody hurried there. That was the secret of the room, and everybody felt it the moment they stepped in.
The little lamp, the knitting, and the family drifting in to be young again.

“The new fashion is to hurry,” Grandma said one night, her needles clicking, “and the old fashion is to care. Hurrying spends you; caring fills you. I have watched this family thirty years, child. The money came and went twice, and the love came and stayed.” Polly sat very still. It seemed to her that the little lamp had lighted the whole world. And the cat, who understood everything, went on sleeping.
Talk together: Grandma says money is weather and love is climate. Do you agree? What in your home is climate?

One by one the family came to her room that winter. More than any theater or party could have drawn them. Fanny unlearned her fine despair there. Tom laid his plans there. And Polly learned, without knowing it, the very words she would want one day soon. They would be wanted when a great question stood knocking at her door. For Grandma’s lamp burned late, and so did her wisdom. It burned for every one of them, and it never once went out. The kettle hummed on its trivet, and Grandma’s needles kept time. Every trouble brought there came out smaller than it went in. Maud learned to knit a garter there. Tom learned to be silent for ten whole minutes, which took longer.

chapters.title: Chapter 16 · Tom's Scrape
chapters.artPrompt: a young man in a dark suit standing before a desk in an office with his head bowed, while an older gray merchant taps a paper, ledger books and a gas lamp on the desk, rain streaming down the dark window behind, heavy evening light, serious storybook illustration

blocks.text: Tom’s good winter had one bad hole in it. A careless friend at the office wanted to borrow money. Tom, warm-hearted and soft-headed, lent his own savings and put his name under his friend’s bill besides. The friend vanished. The bill came due. And Tom walked into his father’s office with the paper in his hand. He carried the truth in his mouth, like a man going to the dentist. And the dentist, this time, was his own father.
The bill lies on the desk between father and son, and the rain runs down the glass.

Mr. Shaw’s anger was a cold thunder, worse than any storm. “Your name is your whole capital, Tom,” he said at last, quietly, which hurt more than shouting. Tom stood it like a man. He gave up his savings. He took on extra work to pay the rest month by month. He wrote honestly to the young man’s family. Then he went, gray-faced, to the one person who never lectured and never spared him either.
Talk together: Tom meant to be kind when he lent and signed. Where did kindness end and foolishness begin?

Polly let him talk it all out. Then she said only: “You have paid a whole year’s wages for one lesson, Tom. Do not waste it by being ashamed forever. Spend it by being wiser instead.” And Tom, who had feared her scorn all the way across town, went home almost cheerful. Scorn had not come, and wisdom had. And somehow the bill seemed smaller already. It took him a year to pay it, and he never missed a month. The friend’s name never came up again, which was a mercy. The family never knew how near they had come to losing Tom’s name in the city. Mr. Shaw heard of it years after, and said nothing then either. Some forgiveness is loudest when it says nothing at all.

chapters.title: Chapter 17 · Polly's Secret
chapters.artPrompt: a young woman in a plain dress standing at her narrow window at dusk looking out over city rooftops with a soft troubled smile, a small stove warming her back, violet evening light over chimneys, tender storybook illustration

blocks.text: Polly had a secret, and she kept it so well that she almost kept it from herself. Her heart had quietly belonged to Tom Shaw for years, since the days of blind-man’s buff and kitchen candy. But Polly was proud in the old-fashioned way. She had nothing but her hands, her music, and her good name. And she would not bring an empty purse into any man’s house. Not even his.
One heart, one small window, and a pride that does not know it is a kind of fear.

Tom, meanwhile, was growing daily more hopeless and more devoted. He came on Sundays with his papers and his troubles. He sat by her small stove, and went home richer than he came. Grandma, knitting in her lamplit corner, watched them both with eyes like still water. “Child,” she said one evening, laying down her needles, “love does not ask what a purse holds. It asks what a heart holds.” And the needles clicked again, softly, like a verdict.
Question for you: Polly will not marry while she is poor. Is that pride, prudence, or a little of both?

Polly said the purse was not the point. The point was that a wife should bring as well as take. Grandma smiled at her needles and said no more. But that night Polly stood a long time at her window, watching the lights come out over the roofs. She knew at last that she was not being noble. She was only being afraid. And love was bigger than her fear. The next Sunday she wore her best dress to meet him, mended at the hem. Tom never saw the mending, only Polly. Tom’s Sundays were the one fixed star of Polly’s week, though she would never have said so. She began, without noticing, to bake on Saturdays. The little stove worked harder than ever, and nobody in the house could think why the muffins had improved.

chapters.title: Chapter 18 · Tom's Question
chapters.artPrompt: a young man in his best dark suit standing very straight in a modest parlor before a young woman in a plain dress, holding both her hands, a small stove and a crooked bookshelf in the room, winter evening light, an old grandmother watching kindly from the doorway, warm storybook illustration

blocks.text: Tom came on a Sunday, in his best suit. His papers were left at home for the first time in years. He stood in Polly’s small parlor as straight as a soldier. His voice shook only a little. “Polly,” he said, “I have loved you since you were fourteen and I was a scamp. I shall never be rich, but I will work for you as long as I live. Will you have me?”
The plainest, oldest question in the world, asked in a small warm room.

Polly gave him both her hands, and the tears stood in her eyes. “Tom,” she said, “I have nothing in the world but my music, my hands, and my heart.” “That is everything,” said Tom. “That is the whole world, Polly. I have known it since the candy-pulling nights.” And so it was settled, as simply as that. It happened in a room with a small stove, with no gold ring and no fine words. And it held, as such things do.
Talk together: Tom and Polly between them own one honest trade, one kind heart, and one small stove. Why does it sound like a fortune?

Grandma, who had seen them come up the stairs together, was ready with her blessing before they could speak. The little Shaw house heard the news at supper. Fanny cried and laughed, and Maud danced round the table. Mr. Shaw said, a little huskily, that Polly was the best bargain his son had ever made. And that he had made it too, long ago. It happened in a marble hall, with a small girl in a quilted hood. Tom held her hands as if they were made of glass and gold at once. Outside, the city went on thundering about its own affairs. Inside, the small stove ticked and settled, like a heart that had made up its mind. And nobody ever asked Polly to explain her happiness, for everybody could see it.

chapters.title: Chapter 19 · The Old-Fashioned Way
chapters.artPrompt: a simple family wedding in a small parlor with a young couple standing before an old grandmother in a lace cap, family and a few friends gathered round, holly on the mantel and a small fire burning, a plain gown and a dark suit, warm golden lamplight, joyful storybook illustration

blocks.text: There was no grand wedding party, for the grand days were over, and nobody missed them. They were married in the small parlor, with the family, a few true friends, and Grandma’s blessing. There were the old words that have joined two lives for a thousand years. Polly wore her plain white muslin. Tom wore his best suit and the proudest face in the city. And the small stove did its very best work.
The old words are said in a small warm room, and they are quite enough.

Afterward there was tea and cake and singing. Mr. Shaw told the story of a stagecoach and a quilted hood till everyone had heard it twice. Fanny had learned to be useful, and managed the household like a general. Maud had learned to be kind. Tom had learned to be true. And Polly had learned, and taught them all, that love is the fortune that never fails. The crooked shelf stood in the corner, holding the singing books, straight enough for that.
Question for you: the Shaws were richest when they were poorest. What did the hard year teach them that money never had?

Whoever visits that house finds the same rule hanging on the wall, in Polly’s neat hand. It says: Keep cheerful, work honestly, care for each other. It is an old-fashioned rule. Fashions change every season, but this one never wears out. And the house where it is kept is always, in all weathers, the warmest one in the street. Which is exactly what Polly’s mother, in her village, had always said it would be. And under the rule, small and neat, Polly had added one more line: with love, P. The wedding cake was small and dark, and Fanny made it herself. It was pronounced the best in the county. Maud strewed paper flowers down the little stair. Grandma sat in the best chair and would not give it up even for the bride.
